questions.question: A distribution has a long tail stretching to the right (a few very large values). How is it described, and how do mean and median compare?
options: Right (positively) skewed, with the mean greater than the median because the tail pulls the mean upward.
Symmetric, with mean equal to median.
Left skewed, with the mean below the median.
Right skewed, with the median above the mean.
questions.explanation: A right-skewed distribution has its long tail on the high side, so the extreme large values drag the mean above the median. Income is a classic example. For left skew the tail is on the low side and the mean sits below the median.
questions.misconception: The skew direction is named for the tail, not the bulk. A long right tail is positive (right) skew.

questions.scenario: You fit a model that assumes normally distributed residuals and want to check that assumption visually before trusting the inference.
questions.question: Which plot is designed for this, and how do you read it?
options: A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot: if the points fall close to the diagonal line, the data matches the reference distribution; systematic curves or S-shapes signal departures.
A single number, the mean of the residuals.
A pie chart of residual signs.
A bar chart of the residuals.
questions.explanation: A QQ plot compares the data's quantiles against a reference distribution's quantiles. Points on the straight diagonal mean a good match; curvature at the ends indicates heavy or light tails, and an S-shape indicates skew. It is the standard visual normality check.
questions.misconception: Normality is a shape question, so a single statistic is not enough. A QQ plot shows where and how the data departs.

questions.question: What does kurtosis describe about a distribution?
options: The heaviness of its tails and the sharpness of its peak relative to a normal distribution.
Its total area, which kurtosis adjusts to 1.
Whether it is skewed left or right.
questions.explanation: Kurtosis measures tail weight and peakedness. High (leptokurtic) means heavy tails and more extreme outliers than a normal; low (platykurtic) means lighter tails. Excess kurtosis subtracts 3 so a normal distribution reads as 0. It is a separate axis from skewness, which measures asymmetry.
